facts.title: Named For Lime Itself
facts.text: Calcium takes its name from the Latin word calx, meaning lime or limestone, the chalky material burned by builders for thousands of years. The element was first isolated in 1808 by the English chemist Humphry Davy, who used electrolysis on a moistened mixture of lime and mercuric oxide. Although ancient civilizations used calcium compounds in mortar and plaster, no one had ever seen the pure metal until Davy's experiments.

facts.title: A Metal You Can Cut
facts.text: Pure calcium is a soft, silvery-white metal that is hard enough to dent but soft enough to cut with a knife. It is surprisingly light for a metal, with a density of about 1.55 grams per cubic centimeter, only a little denser than water. When freshly cut its bright surface quickly dulls as it reacts with oxygen and moisture in the air, forming a grey-white coating of oxide and nitride.

facts.title: The Bone Builder
facts.text: About 99 percent of the calcium in your body is locked inside your bones and teeth as a crystalline mineral called hydroxyapatite. An adult human body contains roughly one kilogram of calcium, making it the most abundant metal in the body by mass. The remaining one percent circulates in blood and cells, where it is so vital that the body will dissolve bone to keep blood levels stable.

facts.title: Sparks Every Heartbeat
facts.text: Calcium ions act as a universal signaling switch inside living cells, triggering muscle contraction, nerve impulses, and the release of hormones. Every single heartbeat depends on a precisely timed surge of calcium ions flooding into heart muscle cells. This is why the concentration of calcium in your blood is kept within an extremely narrow range, controlled by parathyroid hormone and vitamin D.

facts.title: Fifth Most Abundant Element
facts.text: Calcium is the fifth most abundant element in the Earth's crust by mass, at about 4.1 percent, and the third most abundant metal after aluminium and iron. It is far too reactive to exist as a free metal in nature, so it is always found locked in compounds. Vast deposits appear as limestone, marble, chalk, and gypsum, much of it built from the shells and skeletons of ancient sea creatures.

facts.title: Forged In Dying Stars
facts.text: The calcium in your bones was created inside massive stars through nuclear fusion and scattered across space when those stars exploded as supernovae. Calcium is one of the elements astronomers detect most easily in starlight, because its ions produce strong dark lines in stellar spectra known as the Fraunhofer H and K lines. In a real sense, every skeleton on Earth is made of stardust.

facts.title: Burns Brick-Red
facts.text: When a calcium compound is heated in a flame, it glows a distinctive orange-red to brick-red color. Chemists use this flame test to identify the element, and the same effect helps give some red fireworks and emergency flares their warm color. The glow comes from electrons in calcium atoms absorbing heat energy and then releasing it as specific wavelengths of light.

facts.title: It Sweats In Water
facts.text: Drop calcium metal into water and it reacts steadily, fizzing as it releases hydrogen gas and forming calcium hydroxide. The reaction is brisk but gentler than the violent explosions of sodium or potassium, partly because the calcium hydroxide produced is only slightly soluble and coats the metal. This controlled reactivity is one reason calcium sits in the alkaline-earth group rather than the wildly reactive alkali metals.

facts.title: Caves And Cathedrals
facts.text: The stalactites and stalagmites in caves are sculpted over thousands of years by calcium carbonate slowly precipitating from dripping mineral-rich water. The same compound, as limestone and marble, built the Egyptian pyramids, Roman aqueducts, and countless cathedrals. Quicklime made by roasting limestone has been the key ingredient in mortar and cement since antiquity, literally holding civilization together.

facts.title: Steel's Hidden Cleaner
facts.text: Industry uses calcium metal as a powerful reducing agent to extract other metals such as uranium, thorium, and zirconium from their compounds. It is also added to molten steel and aluminium alloys, where it scavenges dissolved oxygen and sulfur to remove impurities and improve quality. This deoxidizing role makes calcium quietly essential to modern metallurgy, even though most of it never appears in the final product.
